Each indicator gets a mark - Risk On, Neutral or Risk Off - from the rules at the bottom of this section. Each index's reading is the mark it has most of; if two marks tie, the more cautious one wins. An indicator that is not available is left out of the count. When the trend marks and the breadth marks point opposite ways (at least 2 of the 3 trend marks Risk On and at least 2 of the 3 breadth marks Risk Off, or the other way round), a short tag under the reading says so: "narrow breadth" or "broad participation".

Risk-On score: each indicator's mark counts 1 for Risk On, 1/2 for Neutral and 0 for Risk Off, every indicator weighted the same; the score is the average, as a percentage (100% = every counted indicator Risk On, 0% = every one Risk Off). It sums up the marks; it is not a probability. One mark moves it about 6 points, so a 5-day average is shown too. The reading above still goes by the most marks, so near a tie the two can differ: 4 Risk On, 1 Neutral and 4 Risk Off scores 50% but reads Risk Off.

Group score: the same marks, averaged inside each group first (Trend, Momentum, Breadth, Volatility), then across the groups. The trend group has three indicators that usually move together, so the Group score gives each group one equal vote. An indicator that is not available is left out of its group. It is shown for comparison only; it is not a probability, and the reading above still goes by the most marks.

CommentaryThe S&P 500 reads Risk On, with 5 Risk On, 4 Neutral and 0 Risk Off marks; its Risk-On score is 78% against a 5-day average of 67%. The Nasdaq reads Neutral, with 3 Risk On, 4 Neutral and 1 Risk Off marks; its score is 63% against a 5-day average of 39%. The VIX at 16.68 marks Risk On, while QQQ at 1.88% below its 20-day average marks Risk Off.

Bull put spread

What this screen looks for: stocks and ETFs priced $20 to $500, above their 50-day average, with options expensive for them (IV Rank over 40, IV Percentile over 50) and heavy trading.

What it is: Sell a put and buy a lower-strike put with the same expiration, collecting a credit. It keeps the credit if the stock stays above the sold strike at expiration.

Main risk: If the stock falls below the bought put, the loss is the gap between the two strikes minus the credit, which is usually several times the credit.

Cash-secured put

What this screen looks for: stocks and ETFs priced $20 to $200, above their 50- and 200-day averages, with options expensive for them (IV Rank over 40, IV Percentile over 50) and heavy trading.

What it is: Sell a put while keeping enough cash to buy 100 shares at the strike, collecting a premium.

Main risk: If the stock falls below the strike, the seller may have to buy 100 shares at the strike, well above the market price; the loss grows the further the stock falls, less only the premium.

Bullish diagonal

What this screen looks for: stocks and ETFs priced $20 to $500, above their 50- and 200-day averages, with options middling for them (IV Rank 20 to 40, IV Percentile 50 to 80) and heavy trading.

What it is: Buy a longer-dated call and sell a shorter-dated call at a higher strike, paying a net debit.

Main risk: A sharp drop in the stock, or a fall in implied volatility, can lose most or all of the debit paid; a sharp rise past the sold strike also cuts into the gain.

Long call

What this screen looks for: stocks and ETFs priced $5 to $500, above their 20- and 50-day averages, with options cheap for them (IV Rank and IV Percentile both under 50) and heavy trading.

What it is: Buy a call, which gains if the stock rises above the strike by more than the price paid, before expiration.

Main risk: If the stock does not rise far enough soon enough, the call loses value every day and can expire worthless: the whole amount paid is lost.

Bear call spread

What this screen looks for: stocks and ETFs priced $20 to $500, below their 20-, 50- and 200-day averages, with options expensive for them (IV Rank over 40, IV Percentile over 50) and heavy trading.

What it is: Sell a call and buy a higher-strike call with the same expiration, collecting a credit. It keeps the credit if the stock stays below the sold strike at expiration.

Main risk: If the stock rises above the bought call, the loss is the gap between the two strikes minus the credit, which is usually several times the credit.

Bearish diagonal

What this screen looks for: stocks and ETFs priced $20 to $500, below their 50- and 200-day averages, with options middling for them (IV Rank 20 to 40, IV Percentile over 50) and heavy trading.

What it is: Buy a longer-dated put and sell a shorter-dated put at a lower strike, paying a net debit.

Main risk: A sharp rise in the stock, or a fall in implied volatility, can lose most or all of the debit paid; a sharp drop past the sold strike also cuts into the gain.

Long put

What this screen looks for: S&P 500 and Nasdaq Composite stocks (no ETFs) priced over $15 that gapped down to a new 5-day low in the latest session, with Barchart's 20-day average signal at Sell and its medium-term signal at Buy, options cheap for them (IV Rank under 45), more than 1,000 option contracts traded and volume above normal.

What it is: Buy a put, which gains if the stock falls below the strike by more than the price paid, before expiration.

Main risk: If the stock does not fall far enough soon enough, the put loses value every day and can expire worthless: the whole amount paid is lost.

No stocks met this screen's conditions today.

Iron condor

What this screen looks for: stocks and ETFs priced $20 to $500 within 2% of their 20-day average, with options fairly expensive for them (IV Rank 40 to 50, IV Percentile over 50), more than 1,000 option contracts traded and volume no more than 20% above normal.

What it is: Sell a put spread below the price and a call spread above it, same expiration, collecting a credit. It keeps the credit if the stock stays between the two sold strikes.

Main risk: A big move either way can reach one of the spreads; the loss is then that spread's width minus the credit, usually several times the credit.

Covered strangle

What this screen looks for: stocks and ETFs priced $20 to $150, above their 50- and 200-day averages, with IV Rank over 30 and IV Percentile over 40, more than 500,000 shares a day on average and more than 500 option contracts traded.

What it is: Own 100 shares, sell a call above the price and sell a put below it, collecting two premiums.

Main risk: If the stock falls, the shares lose value and the put can require buying 100 more shares at its strike, so the loss on a drop is about double that of owning the shares; gains above the call strike are given up.

Ratio call diagonal

What this screen looks for: stocks and ETFs priced $20 to $500, above their 20- and 50-day averages, with IV Rank 30 to 60 and IV Percentile over 40, and heavy trading.

What it is: Buy a longer-dated call and sell more shorter-dated calls than were bought, at a higher strike.

Main risk: The call side sells more options than it buys, so the extra sold calls are uncovered: if the stock rises sharply past the sold strike, losses on that side can be much larger than the premium collected, with no fixed limit.

Bull put spread (earnings)

What this screen looks for: stocks and ETFs priced $20 to $500, above their 50-day average, reporting earnings within the next 14 days, with options expensive for them (IV Rank over 40, IV Percentile over 50), more than 1 million shares a day on average and more than 1,000 option contracts traded.

What it is: A bull put spread (sell a put, buy a lower-strike put, same expiration, for a credit) placed while an earnings report is due.

Main risk: The report can gap the stock below both strikes overnight, giving the full loss (the gap between the strikes minus the credit) with no chance to adjust first.

Bullish diagonal (earnings)

What this screen looks for: stocks (no ETFs) priced $20 to $500, above their 50- and 200-day averages, reporting earnings within the next 30 days, with IV Rank 30 to 40 and IV Percentile over 50, and heavy trading.

What it is: A bullish diagonal (buy a longer-dated call, sell a shorter-dated call at a higher strike, for a debit) placed around an earnings report.

Main risk: Implied volatility usually drops right after the report, which cuts the value of the longer-dated call; a sharp move either way on the report can lose most or all of the debit.

Bearish diagonal (earnings)

What this screen looks for: stocks (no ETFs) priced $20 to $500, below their 50- and 200-day averages, reporting earnings within the next 30 days, with IV Rank 30 to 40 and IV Percentile over 50, and heavy trading.

What it is: A bearish diagonal (buy a longer-dated put, sell a shorter-dated put at a lower strike, for a debit) placed around an earnings report.

Main risk: Implied volatility usually drops right after the report, which cuts the value of the longer-dated put; a sharp move either way on the report can lose most or all of the debit.
